children: By Kim Mackrael
BRUSSELS — Europe is racing to end its reliance on foreign energy by shedding fossil fuels. The problem: Going green is cementing new dependencies on China.

The European Union is quickly adding renewable power to its grid and last year generated more electricity from wind and solar than from fossil fuels. Policymakers hope the rapid shift will ease the bloc's reliance on oil and gas imports and bring down energy prices.
Europe's energy bill jumped after it slashed Russian fuel imports following Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and started importing more U.S. liquefied natural gas.
Chinese equipment is enabling Europe's shift to cleaner technology. It is also putting European companies out of business.

Now European officials are trying to help domestic manufacturers compete. The effort is part of a tougher approach to China in which the EU will cap Chinese hybrid-vehicle imports to reduce its trade deficit, and propose a new legal tool that could allow it to restrict market access in exceptional circumstances.

The EU has also proposed made-in-Europe rules for public contracts involving solar panels, wind turbines and batteries and some governments already offer subsidies for consumers who choose locally-made products. Officials expect the new public contract rules to be negotiated over coming months.

Europe isn't alone. South Korea recently introduced a tax credit for locally-made solar, wind and battery products. Japan, which relies heavily on Chinese solar products, is subsidizing ultrathin solar technology in a bid to challenge China's dominance.

China makes at least 80% of the world's solar products and lithium-ion batteries. Europe is much stronger in domestic wind-turbine production, although its companies depend heavily on China for the rare-earth permanent magnets those turbines use.

Europe faces a tougher trade off than the U.S., which has high tariffs on Chinese solar equipment, electric vehicles and other clean-tech products. America relies less on energy imports because it produces oil and gas domestically. And the Trump administration isn't pursuing the climate goals Europe has embraced.

Still, Swedish electrical installer Hallabro Elektriska says it often struggles to convince customers to go local. Hallabro charges about $16,000 for a standard rooftop solar installation, with a $2,000 premium for European hardware. Installations of European-assembled panels have declined because Chinese alternatives are cheaper and more advanced.
Hallabro has more success with European-made inverters, which convert the electricity that solar panels generate into a usable current.
"There is definitely a gap between the desire to support European industry and actual purchases," Hallabro Chief Executive Emma Elheim Karlsson said.

It isn't only solar. Chinese electric-vehicle brands that are made in China are about 35% cheaper to make than fully European models, according to AlixPartners, a consulting group. Electrolyzers, which use water and electricity to make hydrogen, can be produced in China for less than half of what it costs to make them in Europe, International Energy Agency data shows. Wind-turbine equipment from China can be made for between 30% and 45% cheaper.
Propping up European manufacturers will be costly, economists say, which could slow the adoption of clean technology needed to hit EU climate targets.

If prices go up, "that's of course a disincentive for consumers to switch from carbon-intensive tech to lower-emissions technologies such as EVs and solar panels," said Capital Economics economist Hamad Hussain. "You're likely to get a slower transition."

Solar panels are among the most prominent examples of how Chinese competition has displaced European industry. Europe was once a top global solar producer. But dozens of companies closed during the 2010s and 2020s amid a flood of lower-cost, heavily subsidized Chinese imports, despite several years of European tariffs.
Simone Tagliapietra, deputy director at think tank Bruegel, said Europe's solar experience shows it doesn't make sense to try to compete in every sector.

"Many people use this as an example of the failure of industrial policy in Europe," Tagliapietra said. He said Europe lost some solar manufacturing jobs, but the rapid rollout of low-cost solar panels helped create new installation and maintenance jobs for Europeans and sped up the continent's energy transition.
"These panels are cheap and allow Europe to boost solar energy while cutting our reliance on fossil fuels," he said.
Tagliapietra said it makes more economic sense for Europe to focus on sectors where it still has a comparative advantage, such as cable manufacturing and wind turbines.

National-security concerns pose a thornier problem. The EU earlier this year barred EU-funded projects from using Chinese inverters. The bloc is separately considering rules that could extend that restriction to certain types of grid connections that aren't EU-funded.
Experts consider inverters risky because they could be used by hackers to cause blackouts if a large number are targeted simultaneously.

Austrian inverter maker Fronius says an Austrian government program offering homeowners a rebate for installing European solar products is a positive step, despite an annual cap that has limited its effect.
"Commercially at the moment it doesn't bring so much," Fronius Chief Executive Elisabeth Engelbrechtsmüller-Strauss said of the program. "But it raises awareness that there is an issue."
European lawmakers have separately raised concerns about Chinese electric vehicles and data security. And some clean-tech experts say batteries are crucial for their role in defense and grids.
"This is a new type of dependence," said Joseph Dellatte, a resident fellow with French think tank Institut Montaigne, of Europe's reliance on Chinese clean-tech imports.
"It creates conditions where you could lose industrial skills and industrial knowledge for good."
